doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Benny Goodman stories, Pops and Ziggy Elman mix-up
summary: Gibbs tells absent-minded Benny Goodman stories: the unreturned punchline, calling everyone Pops, and Ziggy Elman confusion, explaining the chapter title El Foggo.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Excellent. When I got to about the middle of the book and I turned the page and I saw the title of the chapter Foggo, I said I know who he’s going to talk about now.

You know everybody has a Benny Goodman story but not everybody living — one of my most fun times is I used to do a lot of the jazz cruises, you know, 90 musicians would be on a cruise. And Mel Powell was on one of the cruises. And Mel Powell worked with Benny Goodman way before I did. And we sat there one night talking about Benny Goodman stories, and who else? Maybe Ken Peplowski, he worked for Benny Goodman. Whoever was there that knew Benny Goodman, and it was actually like a bunch of comedians sitting around telling stories. Because Benny Goodman did in real life what a comedian would write in a skit. It would be like you could write a whole skit on one of these incidents. For example I think I wrote this in the book, he used to love it when I told him jokes. I’m standing on 57th Street and sometimes Benny would be staring me in the eye and you think he’s listening to you but he’s in Pittsburgh. His mind is somewhere else. And I’m telling him this joke and I’m really into it, and I get to the point where it’s the punch line and I’ve got my hands up for the punch line, and he turns around and walks away from me. And I’m standing like this on 57th Street with my hands up in the air. I mean you know before I ever joined Benny Goodman, because I was always a Benny Goodman — I used to love the band, I loved Benny and his playing. I used to hear a story that sounded so farfetched it’s like I’ll tell you a story about someone with a pair of black shoes, and you tell me it to this person, and you tell it to the next person. By the time you get to the seventh person and it come back to me, it was a red shirt, you know. It sounded so farfetched. But after I worked with him I realized every story I had ever heard about him had to be true. And I was [inaudible] because this man was in left field. He’d forget to button his fly before he went on stage or comb his hair. But he could play the clarinet, forget it. He knew, and he called everybody “Pops.” He loved my last name originally, Gubenko, so he called me Gubenko. I’ll tell you how, he couldn’t remember people’s names. One time, I think I wrote about it in the book, he was going to do a tour with Louis Armstrong and the Benny Goodman band. So Joe Glaser, who managed both © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

of them, the agent, he told Joe Glaser, “Get me” this is in New York, “Get me Ziggy Elman.” Ziggy Elman was in California. So I go to the first rehearsal I went with Joe Glaser to Benny’s rehearsal, even though I wasn’t going to be on the show I just wanted to hear the band. And I’m standing with Joe Glaser and Benny looks at me and he says, “I asked you to get me Ziggy Elman on the trumpet” he says. “That’s Ziggy Elman, I flew him in” and Joe Glaser would use every F word in the world, you know I’m telling you, if I told him, he said, “That’s not Ziggy Elman.” “What do you mean not Ziggy Elman?” Ziggy Elman [Goodman] didn’t know the difference between Chris Griffin and Harry James. Everybody was Pops. He didn’t know the difference. He didn’t know your name. And I used to make jokes, he once called his wife “Pops.” At rehearsal, up where he lived, his wife came in, she was in the other room, she said, “Benny, should I bring the guys some Cokes” or something. He says, “Oh not now, Pops.” You know? We always said you can imagine what it would be like when he was making love to her, what he called her. “Hey Pops.”
Yeah, you know. Well he was foggy. He was in left field. And the reason I entitled a second chapter “El Foggo Rides Again” because of the title of that song, “Benny Rides Again.” You know.
